<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A5" title="In Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">E </span>Pseudo-code of the training procedure</span></a></li>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A7" title="In Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">G </span>Posterior inference details</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_appendix">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening (DABS), a method for performing adaptive factorial screening in high-dimensional discrete design spaces. DABS learns a policy network offline to sequentially select informative experiments, amortizing Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design. It handles binary designs, incorporates sparsity and interactions via a spike-and-slab prior with strong heredity. The model is trained using a contrastive lower bound on information about factor activity with nuisance effect sizes and noise variance analytically integrated out. Unlike prior amortized Bayesian design approaches, DABS also integrates Gibbs posterior inference at deployment, yielding posterior probabilities of factor activity and credible intervals on effect sizes. We demonstrate DABS on screening problems calibrated to real-world benchmarks and show it achieves superior accuracy and scalability over classical and Bayesian baselines under tight experimental budgets.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Designing experiments to efficiently explore high-dimensional input spaces is a central challenge in many areas of science and engineering. In particular, screening designs aim to identify the subset of most influential factors among a large number of candidates while minimizing the number of required experimental runs. For instance, in early-stage drug development, researchers must determine which formulation and process variables most strongly affect key quality attributes such as dissolution or stability. When many factors are potentially relevant (say, 12 factors at 2 levels), exploring all possible combinations would require <math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{12}=4096" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>12</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4096</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{12}=4096</annotation></semantics></math> experimental runs, which is prohibitively expensive in practice. This combinatorial explosion motivates the use of screening strategies to reduce experimental cost while focusing attention on the variables that drive system performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Classical screening designs are typically non-adaptive and specified a priori (e.g. Plackett-Burman <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Plackett and J.P., 1946</a>)</cite>, fractional factorial <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Montgomery, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Box et al., 2005</a>)</cite> or D-optimal designs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mitchell, 1974</a>)</cite>). Factor significance is then assessed post hoc using frequentist tools such as t-tests or ANOVA. These designs are derived to minimise parameter-estimation variance under a fixed assumed model, rather than to directly target the binary active/inactive decision that screening ultimately requires, and they neither incorporate prior knowledge nor adapt to observed data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To overcome these limitations, Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chaloner and Verdinelli, 1995</a>)</cite> offers a way to incorporate prior knowledge about factor importance and to select configurations adaptively that maximise the expected information gain about the active factors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In the sequential setting, this corresponds to selecting each new experiment to maximise the mutual information between its outcome and the set of active factors, conditioned on the history of past experiments and responses.
However, this requires repeated posterior inference and optimization of an acquisition function (i.e., an information-based utility used to select the next experiment), which is often computationally prohibitive in real-time screening campaigns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ryan et al., 2016</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Deep Adaptive Design (DAD) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foster et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and related extensions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivanova et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Poole et al., 2019</a>)</cite> remove this computational burden by training a neural policy network offline on thousands of simulated experimental trajectories. At deployment time, the policy produces the next configuration via a single forward pass, amortizing all optimization. However, these methods target parameter inference rather than active-set recovery and provide no mechanism for posterior inference over factor activity or effect-size credible intervals once the experiments are complete. They are also formulated for continuous design spaces, which requires an additional adaptation step for discrete factorial settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To address this gap, we introduce DABS (Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening). DABS trains a deep policy network entirely offline using simulated trajectories from a discrete design space and complements it with a Gibbs sampler for posterior inference over active factors and effect sizes, leveraging closed-form Student-t full conditionals derived from the conjugate spike-and-slab model. The contributions of this paper are threefold. (i) We derive a screening-specific training objective that targets the mutual information between the experimental history and the active-set indicators, with the continuous effect sizes and noise variance marginalised out analytically. This focuses the policy on the screening decision. Effect sizes for the retained factors are recovered analytically at deployment. (ii) We embed screening structure directly into the amortized design framework via a spike-and-slab prior with strong heredity on two-way interactions, so that the offline-trained policy produces designs calibrated to the sparsity and hierarchy of real screening problems. (iii) We couple the amortized policy with a closed-form Gibbs sampler at deployment that exploits the same Student-<math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> full conditionals, yielding posterior probabilities of factor activity and credible intervals on effect sizes from a single pass through the data, a capability absent from standard policy-based BOED pipelines.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Sequential Bayesian Experimental Design</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> denote an unknown parameter vector with prior <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>. In a sequential experiment, at step <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, a single new design <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is selected based on the history <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t-1}=\{(\xi_{s},y_{s})\}_{s=1}^{t-1}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t-1}=\{(\xi_{s},y_{s})\}_{s=1}^{t-1},</annotation></semantics></math>
and a scalar response <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is observed. The informativeness of a candidate design is quantified by the conditional mutual information between <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> and the observation <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lindley, 1955</a>)</cite>:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="I(\theta;y_{t}\mid h_{t-1},\xi_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim p(\theta\mid h_{t-1}),\,y_{t}\sim <td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The ratio inside the logarithm compares the likelihood under a specific parameter realization <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> with the marginal likelihood averaged over all possible parameter values.
This quantity corresponds to the expected reduction in posterior entropy about <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> after observing <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Higher values indicate more informative experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A design policy <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>, parametrized by a neural network with parameters <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>, selects experiments adaptively via
<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\xi_{t}\sim\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid h_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{t}\sim\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid h_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math>. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foster et al. (2021)</a></cite>, the cumulative expected information gain over an experimental sequence decomposes as</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{J}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim p(\theta),h_{T}\sim p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi_{\phi})}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}I(\theta;y_{t}\mid h_{t-1},\xi_{t})\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒥</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{J}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim p(\theta),h_{T}\sim p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi_{\phi})}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}I(\theta;y_{t}\mid h_{t-1},\xi_{t})\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Maximizing cumulative information gain rather than a single-step criterion encourages globally informative experimental sequences and enables the design policy to account for long-term effects of sequential decisions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Contrastive Estimation of Information Gain</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Direct maximisation of <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{J}(\phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒥</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{J}(\phi)</annotation></semantics></math> is intractable because evaluating the marginal likelihood</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(y_{t}\mid h_{t-1},\xi_{t})=\int p(y_{t}\mid\theta,\xi_{t})\,p(\theta\mid h_{t-1})\,d\theta" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(y_{t}\mid h_{t-1},\xi_{t})=\int p(y_{t}\mid\theta,\xi_{t})\,p(\theta\mid h_{t-1})\,d\theta</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">requires integration over the parameter posterior <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\theta\mid h_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\theta\mid h_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math> at every step. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foster et al. (2021)</a></cite> address this with a Monte Carlo lower bound that replaces the intractable marginal <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(h_{T}\mid\pi_{\phi})=\int p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi_{\phi})\,p(\theta)\,d\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(h_{T}\mid\pi_{\phi})=\int p(h_{T}\mid\theta,\pi_{\phi})\,p(\theta)\,d\theta</annotation></semantics></math> by an empirical average over <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> contrastive samples drawn from the prior, building on earlier stochastic-gradient BOED <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foster et al., 2019b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{0}\sim p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{0}\sim p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> denote the parameter sample that generates the trajectory <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, and let <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{L}\sim p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{L}\sim p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> denote <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> independent contrastive samples from the prior. The sequential Prior Contrastive Estimation (sPCE) bound is</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\text{sPCE}_{L}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{0}\sim p(\theta),\ h_{T}\sim p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{0},\pi_{\phi}),\ \theta_{1:L}\sim p(\theta)}\left[\log\frac{p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{0})}{\frac{1}{L+1}\sum_{i=0}^{L}p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{i})}\right]\leq\mathcal{J}(\phi)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mtext>sPCE</mtext><mi>L</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>θ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo rspace="0.577em">,</mo><mi>h</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>θ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo rspace="0.577em">,</mo><mi>θ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><mi>log</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒥</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{sPCE}_{L}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{0}\sim p(\theta),\ h_{T}\sim p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{0},\pi_{\phi}),\ \theta_{1:L}\sim p(\theta)}\left[\log\frac{p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{0})}{\frac{1}{L+1}\sum_{i=0}^{L}p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{i})}\right]\leq\mathcal{J}(\phi),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where the expectation is over <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{0}\sim p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{0}\sim p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>, the trajectory <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{T}\sim p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{0},\pi_{\phi})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{T}\sim p(h_{T}\mid\theta_{0},\pi_{\phi})</annotation></semantics></math>, and the contrastive draws <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\theta_{1:L}\sim p(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{1:L}\sim p(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>. A corresponding upper bound yields the sandwich relation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rainforth et al., 2018</a>)</cite></p>
<table id="S2.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{sPCE}_{L}(\phi)\leq\mathcal{J}(\phi)\leq\text{sNMC}_{L}(\phi)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mtext>sPCE</mtext><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒥</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>sNMC</mtext><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{sPCE}_{L}(\phi)\leq\mathcal{J}(\phi)\leq\text{sNMC}_{L}(\phi),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">with both bounds converging to <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{J}(\phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒥</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{J}(\phi)</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. The sPCE bound serves as the training objective. The sequential Nested Monte Carlo (sNMC) bound is used at evaluation time to verify tightness of the trained policy.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Problem Setup and Factorial Screening Model</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Consider a screening experiment with <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> factors, each set to a high or low level at every experimental run <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Montgomery, 2017</a>)</cite>.
The objective is to identify the active set from as few experiments as possible, together with credible intervals on the magnitudes of the corresponding effects. At step <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1,\ldots,T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1,\ldots,T</annotation></semantics></math>, a design vector <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{t}=(\xi_{t,1},...,\xi_{t,p})\in\{-1,+1\}^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{t}=(\xi_{t,1},...,\xi_{t,p})\in\{-1,+1\}^{p}</annotation></semantics></math> is selected where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{t,k}=+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{t,k}=+1</annotation></semantics></math> (resp. <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math>) indicates that factor <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is set to its high (resp. low) level and a scalar response is observed:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="y_{t}=f(\xi_{t},\theta)+\varepsilon_{t},\quad\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}),\quad\sigma^{2}\sim\mathrm{Inv\text{-}Gamma}(\alpha_{0},\beta_{0}),\quad\alpha_{0},\beta_{0}&gt;0," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>∼</mo><mi>Inv</mi><mtext>-</mtext><mi>Gamma</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t}=f(\xi_{t},\theta)+\varepsilon_{t},\quad\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}),\quad\sigma^{2}\sim\mathrm{Inv\text{-}Gamma}(\alpha_{0},\beta_{0}),\quad\alpha_{0},\beta_{0}&gt;0,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">with the conjugate inverse-gamma prior on <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> enabling the analytical marginalization described in Section 3.2. The parameter vector <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=(z,\beta,\sigma^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=(z,\beta,\sigma^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> combines binary activity indicators <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\in\{0,1\}^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\in\{0,1\}^{p}</annotation></semantics></math>, continuous effect sizes <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{p}</annotation></semantics></math> and the noise variance. An indicator <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{k}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{k}=1</annotation></semantics></math> (resp. <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>) denotes that factor <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is active (resp. inactive) and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> determines the magnitude of its contribution. While we restrict attention to binary designs <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{t}\in\{-1,+1\}^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{t}\in\{-1,+1\}^{p}</annotation></semantics></math>, this is not a limitation. For models that are linear in the inputs <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math>, optimal designs over the hypercube <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,1]^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,1]^{p}</annotation></semantics></math> are attained at the vertices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 1.</span> <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Consider a linear–Gaussian model with design space <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi\in[-1,1]^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ξ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi\in[-1,1]^{p}</annotation></semantics></math>. For information-theoretic design criteria that depend on <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math> through quadratic forms, there exists an optimal design in <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{-1,+1\}^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{-1,+1\}^{p}</annotation></semantics></math>.</em>
A proof is provided in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Proof of Proposition 1 ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Screening experiments rely on the factor sparsity principle <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Box and Meyer, 1986</a>)</cite>, which posits that generally only a small subset of factors significantly influence the response. This assumption is encoded through a spike-and-slab prior on the effect sizes, which is a standard approach for Bayesian variable selection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ishwaran and Rao, 2005</a>)</cite>:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a,b),\qquad z_{k}\mid\rho\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\rho),\qquad\beta_{k}\mid z_{k},\sigma^{2}\sim\begin{cases}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\ \tau_{\text{active}}^{2}),&amp;z_{k}=1,\\
\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\tau_{\text{inactive}}^{2}),&amp;z_{k}=0.\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>Beta</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>Bernoulli</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mtext>active</mtext><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mtext>inactive</mtext><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a,b),\qquad z_{k}\mid\rho\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\rho),\qquad\beta_{k}\mid z_{k},\sigma^{2}\sim\begin{cases}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\ \tau_{\text{active}}^{2}),&amp;z_{k}=1,\\
\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\tau_{\text{inactive}}^{2}),&amp;z_{k}=0.\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\in(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\in(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math> is the prior probability that a factor is active, drawn from a <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Beta</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)</annotation></semantics></math> hyperprior with prior mean <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}[\rho]=a/(a+b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}[\rho]=a/(a+b)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{2}_{\text{active}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mtext>active</mtext><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{2}_{\text{active}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the variance for active effects, and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{2}_{\text{inactive}}\ll\tau^{2}_{\text{active}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mtext>inactive</mtext><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>≪</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mtext>active</mtext><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{2}_{\text{inactive}}\ll\tau^{2}_{\text{active}}</annotation></semantics></math> shrinks inactive effects toward zero.
Besides main effects, pairwise interactions between factors, which capture joint effects beyond individual contributions, are also considered. Each interaction between factors <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> is associated with an effect size <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> and an activity indicator <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math>. To reflect the structure typically assumed in screening experiments, we impose the strong heredity principle <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hamada and Wu, 1992</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu and Hamada, 2009</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chipman, 1996</a>)</cite>, meaning that an interaction between factors <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> can only be active if both parent main effects are active. The hyperparameter <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\mathrm{int}}\in(0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>int</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\mathrm{int}}\in(0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> is the conditional probability that a heredity-allowed interaction is active:</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="z_{ij}\mid z_{i},z_{j}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{\mathrm{int}}\cdot z_{i}z_{j}),\qquad\beta_{ij}\mid z_{ij},\sigma^{2}\sim\begin{cases}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\tau_{\text{active}}^{2}),&amp;z_{ij}=1,\\
\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\tau_{\text{inactive}}^{2}),&amp;z_{ij}=0.\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em"
