class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS6.p3.pic1.17" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">20</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><path style="fill:none" d="M 0 196.85 L -3.15 196.85"></path><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -19.07 193.73)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:1em;--ltx-fo-height:0.57em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:7.97pt;" height="6.24" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 6.24)" width="11.03"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS6.p3.pic1.18" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">25</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</span>
<span id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<span class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>The wedge prediction: below the boundary <math id="S3.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=p</annotation></semantics></math>, DABS opens an advantage over the optimal static design, with arrows marking each case study’s sweep.</span>
</span></span>

<span id="S3.SS6.p3.1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_middle" style="width:211.4pt;">
<span id="S3.SS6.p3.1.2.1" class="ltx_p">The adaptive term <math id="S3.SS6.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(z;h_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(z;h_{T})</annotation></semantics></math> is bounded above by the identifiability dimension of <math id="S3.SS6.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>. When the budget <math id="S3.SS6.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is large relative to this dimension, the design has enough capacity to span the coordinate directions required to resolve <math id="S3.SS6.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>, and no fixed-versus-adaptive gap remains. Below this identifiability boundary, DABS can use early observations to identify candidate actives and steer subsequent queries into the relevant subspace, while a static policy must commit to a <math id="S3.SS6.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional measurement subspace before any data are observed. This predicts a wedge in the <math id="S3.SS6.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(p,T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(p,T)</annotation></semantics></math> plane, illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.6 When Does Adaptivity Help ‣ 3 Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. The experiments of Section 5 test this prediction along complementary axes: sweeping <math id="S3.SS6.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> at fixed <math id="S3.SS6.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> (Section 5.2), sweeping <math id="S3.SS6.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> at fixed <math id="S3.SS6.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> (Section 5.3), and sweeping <math id="S3.SS6.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> at three problem sizes under strong-heredity interaction recovery (Section 5.4).</span>
</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Related work</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Screening designs are a core component of design of experiments for efficiently identifying active factors with few runs. Traditional methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guptha et al., 2025</a>)</cite> (fractional factorial <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Box et al., 2005</a>)</cite>, Plackett-Burman <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Plackett and J.P., 1946</a>)</cite> and supersaturated designs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang, 1967</a>)</cite>) focus on estimating main effects and, when resolution permits, interactions under sparsity assumptions. These methods are non-adaptive by construction: the experimental plan is fixed before any observations are collected. When the goal is to identify active factors under a tight budget, this static structure can be inefficient, as it allocates runs uniformly without exploiting the sparsity of the active set <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ravi et al., 2016</a>)</cite>, and ignores information that early observations provide about uninformative directions.
Bayesian screening methods instead quantify uncertainty over the active-factor set and model sparsity explicitly through priors such as spike-and-slab <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mitchell and Beauchamp, 1986</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">George and McCulloch, 1997</a>)</cite> or horseshoe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">O’Hara and Sillanpää, 2009</a>)</cite>. These methods focus on posterior inference and variable selection but typically assume a fixed experimental design. Recent work extends these ideas to ultra-high-dimensional regression <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Run et al., 2025</a>)</cite> or double-robust variable selection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Linhan et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. The foundational framework for sequential experiment selection is provided by Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design formalized by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chaloner and Verdinelli (1995)</a></cite>, which selects experiments by maximizing an information theoretic utility. However, in practice, these methods are not amortized: each new experiment requires an expensive optimization step at decision time <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Poole et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Butakov et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, limiting use in sequential settings. A widely used simplification of classical BOED is greedy one-step lookahead <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jones et al., 1998</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foster et al., 2019a</a>)</cite>, which we use as the Myopic baseline in Section 5.1.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Amortized policy-based Bayesian experimental design was introduced with Deep Adaptive Design (DAD) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foster et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and its likelihood-free extension iDAD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivanova et al., 2021</a>)</cite> (we do not adopt this variant, see Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I On the use of implicit DAD (iDAD) ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>), which learn a policy offline to map past observations to new experimental designs. This avoids the expensive per-step optimization required by classical Bayesian optimal experimental design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chaloner and Verdinelli, 1995</a>)</cite>. Subsequent work extends this framework to continuous dynamical systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Strouwen and Micluta-Câmpeanu, 2026</a>)</cite>. These methods optimize cumulative information gain during training. Posterior inference at deployment is typically delegated to a separate mechanism <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Recent work has explored targeted experimental design objectives that focus on specific functionals of the parameters rather than total information (e.g., contextual optimization in CO-BED <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivanova et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, predictive information gain in EPIG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bickford Smith et al., 2023</a>)</cite>). In contrast, we target information about the support indicators of active factors. However, existing amortized approaches were developed for continuous-parameter estimation and do not incorporate the sparsity or heredity structure of screening problems. Adapting them to the discrete factorial regime with binary designs <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{-1,+1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{-1,+1\}</annotation></semantics></math>, strong-heredity interactions, and tight experimental budgets <math id="S4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\ll p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\ll p</annotation></semantics></math> is the gap we address.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate DABS on three published screening benchmarks calibrated to real-world experimental settings and compare it against four baselines spanning Bayesian design, classical DoE, and adaptive sensing. The benchmarks are chosen to test the wedge prediction of Section 3 across complementary directions. We first describe the evaluation protocol before introducing the case studies and baselines.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Every experiment reports F1, true positive rate (TPR) and false discovery rate (FDR) computed from the Gibbs decoder at posterior inclusion threshold 0.5. Metrics are reported separately for main effects and two-factor interactions. Error bars denote <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> confidence intervals over five independent random seeds for each <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(p,T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(p,T)</annotation></semantics></math> setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Section 3 predicts that adaptivity is beneficial only when the experimental budget <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is insufficient to identify the active set <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>. Once this identifiability boundary is crossed, adaptive and optimal fixed designs should perform similarly because, under the linear-Gaussian model, adaptation cannot improve estimation of effect sizes conditional on <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lindley, 1955</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chaloner and Verdinelli, 1995</a>)</cite>. The experiments below test this prediction by varying either the experimental budget or the problem size.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We consider three published screening benchmarks. For each benchmark, we simulate responses under the model of Section 3 with hyperparameters calibrated to the published problem. Case Study 1 uses the biotechnological benchmark of inulinase production by <span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A. niger</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Poorna and Kulkarni, 1995</a>)</cite>, with <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=15</annotation></semantics></math> candidate factors and three active main effects, while varying <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> from 4 to 16. Case Study 2 uses the biomedical benchmark of hematopoietic stem-cell expansion in cord blood <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2004</a>)</cite>, fixing <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=16</annotation></semantics></math> and increasing <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> from 10 to 26, causing the expected number of active factors to grow from roughly four to ten. Case Study 3 uses the metallurgical benchmark of electrochemical dissolution of GH4738 nickel-based superalloy scrap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, containing four active main effects and three two-factor interactions under strong heredity. Here we vary <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in\{4,6,8\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\in\{4,6,8\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We compare DABS with four baselines. The <em id="S5.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">static design</em> is the optimal fixed design under the same Bayesian model and sPCE objective, isolating the benefit of adaptivity. The <em id="S5.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Plackett–Burman</em> design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Plackett and J.P., 1946</a>)</cite> provides the standard orthogonal fractional-factorial baseline. The <em id="S5.SS1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">myopic</em> baseline greedily maximises one-step expected information gain under the same Bayesian model, isolating the value of the learned policy. Finally, the <em id="S5.SS1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">multi-stage adaptive</em> baseline from compressed sensing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Haupt et al., 2011</a>)</cite> iteratively prunes candidate factors using marginal-effect estimates. The static and myopic methods therefore serve as matched Bayesian controls, while the latter two compare DABS against established approaches from neighbouring literatures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Code, model checkpoints and evaluation scripts are available from the author.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Main effects screening (biotechnology benchmark)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This first case study considers the biotechnological benchmark of inulinase production by A. niger <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Poorna and Kulkarni, 1995</a>)</cite>. The experiment involves <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=15</annotation></semantics></math> controllable factors: four carbon sources (glucose <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, fructose <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, inulin <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, sucrose <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{4}</annotation></semantics></math>), eight nitrogen sources (<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{5},\ldots,X_{12}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>12</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{5},\ldots,X_{12}</annotation></semantics></math>, including yeast extract <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> and peptone <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{6}</annotation></semantics></math>), medium pH (<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{13}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>13</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{13}</annotation></semantics></math>), inoculum level (<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{14}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>14</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{14}</annotation></semantics></math>), and trace element concentration (<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{15}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>15</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{15}</annotation></semantics></math>). The published analysis identifies <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{13}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>13</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{13}</annotation></semantics></math> as the three factors with a statistically significant effect on inulinase activity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We simulate data from the spike-and-slab model of Section 3 with <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(2,8)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>Beta</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(2,8)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\text{active}}=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>active</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\text{active}}=1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\text{inactive}}=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>inactive</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\text{inactive}}=0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S5.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{SNR}=\tau_{\text{active}}^{2}/\sigma^{2}=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>SNR</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mtext>active</mtext><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{SNR}=\tau_{\text{active}}^{2}/\sigma^{2}=4</annotation></semantics></math>). The budget is swept over <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\in\{4,6,8,10,12,14,16\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\in\{4,6,8,10,12,14,16\}</annotation></semantics></math>, spanning the under-identified regime <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T&lt;p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T&lt;p</annotation></semantics></math> and reaching the identifiability boundary <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=p=15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=p=15</annotation></semantics></math>. For each <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(T,\text{seed})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>seed</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(T,\text{seed})</annotation></semantics></math> cell, we train one DABS policy, evaluated over 100 rollouts on main-effect F1 and TPR. FDR curves are reported in Appendix <a href="#A8.SS1" title="H.1 Case Study 1: biotechnology benchmark (main effects, 𝑇 sweep at 𝑝=15) ‣ Appendix H Extended case study results ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<table id="S5.F3.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">

</table></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Main-effect F1 (left) and TPR (right) versus budget <math id="S5.F3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=15</annotation></semantics></math>. Bands are 95% CIs over 5 seeds.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Main effects screening (biotechnology benchmark) ‣ 5 Results ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows main-effect F1 (left) and TPR (right) versus the budget <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>. In the deep-screening regime at <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\leq 6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\leq 6</annotation></semantics></math>, all adaptive methods dominate the static design. At <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=4</annotation></semantics></math>, static F1 is <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.03" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.03</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.03</annotation></semantics></math> against <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.16</annotation></semantics></math> for DABS, <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.24" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.24</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.24</annotation></semantics></math> for the myopic baseline and <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.26" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.26</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.26</annotation></semantics></math> for the multi-stage adaptive baseline. Three of five static seeds collapse to F1 below <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.05</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05</annotation></semantics></math>: the sPCE-optimised batch cannot commit to an informative measurement direction without observed responses. Notably, DABS does not lead the adaptive methods. At the smallest budgets, per-instance greedy selection exploits the available observations faster than the amortised policy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">At <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=8</annotation></semantics></math>, DABS pulls ahead of every baseline for the first time, reaching F1 <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.45" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.45</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.45</annotation></semantics></math> against <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.42" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.42</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.42</annotation></semantics></math> (myopic), <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.41" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.41</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.41</annotation></semantics></math> (static), and <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.36" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.36</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.36</annotation></semantics></math> (multi-stage adaptive). This is the crossover where the amortised policy’s ability to plan ahead more than one step becomes decisive. From <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=10</annotation></semantics></math> onward, DABS and the static design are statistically indistinguishable: at <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=16</annotation></semantics></math> they reach <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.78" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.78</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.78</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.80</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.80</annotation></semantics></math> respectively with overlapping CIs, matching the wedge prediction that no adaptive gain remains once <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> clears the identifiability boundary. The two Bayesian arms then jointly dominate the non-Bayesian baselines: myopic F1 flattens at approximately <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.62" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.62</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.62</annotation></semantics></math>, Plackett-Burman reaches <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.48" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.48</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.48</annotation></semantics></math> at its native <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=16</annotation></semantics></math>, and multi-stage adaptive plateaus at approximately <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.36" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.36</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.36</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=8</annotation></semantics></math> onwards. The comparison with Plackett–Burman and the multi-stage adaptive baseline measures the value of the Bayesian modelling framework, whereas the comparison with the myopic baseline isolates the additional benefit of amortised long-horizon planning over greedy one-step experimental selection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">This convergence matches the wedge prediction of Section 5.1 (formally derived in Section 3.6): once <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> clears the identifiability dimension of <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>, static and adaptive designs achieve the same expected information gain and DABS’ advantage collapses. Once trained, DABS produces each design in a single forward pass, at the marginal cost of a precomputed static design. Timing is reported in Appendix <a href="#A10" title="Appendix J Result details and discussion ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></a> and a single-rollout visualisation in Appendix <a href="#A11" title="Appendix K Visualisation of adaptive behaviour ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">K</span></a>. The same pattern of adaptive dominance below the identifiability boundary and convergence above it appears in the next two case studies (Sections 5.3 and 5.4).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Scaling with the number of factors (HSC expansion benchmark)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This second case study considers the ex vivo expansion of human hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) from umbilical cord blood <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2004</a>)</cite>, a clinically important process bottlenecked by cord-blood availability. The yield depends on the composition of the culture medium, which combines serum substitutes (bovine serum albumin, insulin, transferrin) with ten candidate cytokines including stem cell factor (SCF), Flt-3 ligand (FL), interleukin-3 (IL-3), and thrombopoietin (TPO). Cytokines are expensive to procure and biologically active, so both false positives and false negatives carry real cost. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al. (2004)</a></cite> used a <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{10-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{10-6}</annotation></semantics></math> fractional factorial design with <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=16</annotation></semantics></math> runs to screen all ten candidates and identified four cytokines (SCF, FL, IL-3, TPO) as the dominant drivers of expansion, later confirmed by follow-up optimisation studies. Full simulation details are in Appendix <a href="#A10" title="Appendix J Result details and discussion ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We simulate data from the spike-and-slab model of Section 3 with <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\text{active}}=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>active</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\text{active}}=1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\text{inactive}}=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>inactive</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\text{inactive}}=0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{SNR}=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>SNR</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{SNR}=4</annotation></semantics></math>), and <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(4,6)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>Beta</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(4,6)</annotation></semantics></math> (prior mean 0.4). At the fixed budget <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=16</annotation></semantics></math> of the original Yao et al. design, we vary <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in\{10,12,14,15,16,18,20,22,24,26\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>26</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\in\{10,12,14,15,16,18,20,22,24,26\}</annotation></semantics></math>. The expected number of active main effects grows from 4 at <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=10</annotation></semantics></math> to 10.4 at <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=26" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>26</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=26</annotation></semantics></math>, and the budget crosses the number of candidate factors at <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=T=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=T=16</annotation></semantics></math>, the boundary between the identifiable and under-identified regimes. The sweep stops at <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=26" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>26</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=26</annotation></semantics></math> because the sufficient-statistics encoder, whose input dimension grows as <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(p^{4})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(p^{4})</annotation></semantics></math>, exceeds our GPU memory budget beyond this point. Each policy is evaluated over 100 rollouts on main-effect F1 and FDR. TPR curves are reported in Appendix <a href="#A8.SS2" title="H.2 Case Study 2: HSC benchmark (main effects, 𝑝 sweep at 𝑇=16) ‣ Appendix H Extended case study results ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The four baselines are as defined in Section 5.1. The 16-run Plackett-Burman (PB) design is only applicable for <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\leq 15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\leq 15</annotation></semantics></math> since a <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>-run PB design requires <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\geq p+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\geq p+1</annotation></semantics></math>. Consequently, no PB results are reported for <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\geq 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\geq 16</annotation></semantics></math>. The static, DABS, myopic and multi-stage adaptive methods remain applicable across the full sweep.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<table id="S5.F4.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S5.F4.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.F4.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">

</table></td>
<td id="S5.F4.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">
