</table></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Main-effect F1 (left) and FDR (right) versus <math id="S5.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.F4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=16</annotation></semantics></math>. Bands are 95% CIs over 5 seeds.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Scaling with the number of factors (HSC expansion benchmark) ‣ 5 Results ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (left) shows main-effect F1 as a function of <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. Below the boundary <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\leq 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\leq 16</annotation></semantics></math>, DABS and the static design are statistically indistinguishable, matching the wedge prediction that no adaptive gain remains when <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\geq p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\geq p</annotation></semantics></math>. The myopic baseline reaches a slightly higher F1 in this regime (0.62 to 0.72), Plackett-Burman trails at 0.48 to 0.62 and multi-stage adaptive plateaus around 0.35 to 0.43. From <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=18" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=18</annotation></semantics></math> onwards the picture changes: DABS sits above every baseline, reaching F1 <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.52" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.52</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.52</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=26" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>26</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=26</annotation></semantics></math> against <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.47" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.47</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.47</annotation></semantics></math> (static), <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.43" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.43</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.43</annotation></semantics></math> (myopic), and <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.39" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.39</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.39</annotation></semantics></math> (multi-stage adaptive), with non-overlapping confidence intervals against the static design. Plackett-Burman is inapplicable above <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=15</annotation></semantics></math>. Multi-stage adaptive stays flat throughout, unable to convert additional budget into wider active-set search. The pattern mirrors the wedge from Case Study 1: the adaptive gain of DABS opens when the design is structurally information-starved, which here corresponds to <math id="S5.SS3.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&gt;T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&gt;T</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Scaling with the number of factors (HSC expansion benchmark) ‣ 5 Results ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (right) shows main-effect FDR. In the identifiable regime <math id="S5.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\leq 15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\leq 15</annotation></semantics></math>, the myopic baseline achieves the lowest FDR (0.16 to 0.27), followed by DABS (0.18 to 0.29), the static design (0.20 to 0.34), multi-stage adaptive (0.27 to 0.33), and Plackett-Burman (0.29 to 0.42). From <math id="S5.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=16</annotation></semantics></math> onwards the ordering shifts. DABS’ FDR flattens around 0.32 to 0.35, the static baseline climbs from 0.35 to 0.44, and the myopic baseline degrades from 0.29 to 0.40. At <math id="S5.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=26" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>26</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=26</annotation></semantics></math> DABS achieves an FDR of <math id="S5.SS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.35" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.35</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.35</annotation></semantics></math> against <math id="S5.SS3.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.44" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.44</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.44</annotation></semantics></math> for the static design, a nine-percentage-point improvement. Multi-stage adaptive drifts in the opposite direction, dropping to about <math id="S5.SS3.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.30</annotation></semantics></math> in the middle of the sweep.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The mechanism is asymmetric. The static design must distribute its budget uniformly across all <math id="S5.SS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> candidates because it has no information about which ones are active. As <math id="S5.SS3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> grows, each coordinate receives less measurement effort and the posterior becomes weakly informative for a larger fraction of candidates. The Gibbs decoder, applied with threshold <math id="S5.SS3.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math>, then commits to false positives among the uncertain inactives. DABS instead uses early observations to suppress probing on coordinates that show no evidence of activity, and concentrates the remaining budget on the suspected active subset. The FDR gap over the static baseline drives the F1 gap of Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Scaling with the number of factors (HSC expansion benchmark) ‣ 5 Results ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (left).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Together, Sections 5.2 and 5.3 characterize the screening-regime advantage of DABS along two complementary axes. Section 5.2 varied the budget <math id="S5.SS3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> at fixed <math id="S5.SS3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=15</annotation></semantics></math> and showed adaptive gains that are largest at small <math id="S5.SS3.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> and close as <math id="S5.SS3.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> approaches <math id="S5.SS3.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. Section 5.3 fixed the budget at <math id="S5.SS3.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=16</annotation></semantics></math> and varied <math id="S5.SS3.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>, showing gains that open at <math id="S5.SS3.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\geq T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\geq T</annotation></semantics></math> and grow with the over-parameterization ratio. Both axes confirm that DABS dominates when the design is structurally information-starved. Section 5.4 turns to a different question: whether the same adaptive advantage extends to two-factor interaction recovery under a strict experimental budget.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Two-factor interaction screening (metallurgical benchmark)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This third case study considers the electrochemical dissolution of GH4738 nickel-based superalloy scrap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The process is governed by <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=8</annotation></semantics></math> parameters, of which four are the active main effects: current density (<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>), H<sub id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub">2</sub>SO<sub id="S5.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sub">4</sub> concentration (<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>), NiCl<sub id="S5.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_sub">2</sub> concentration (<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{4}</annotation></semantics></math>) and electrolysis time (<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{6}</annotation></semantics></math>). Prior analysis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> identifies three significant two-factor interactions, <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{1}X_{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>6</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{1}X_{6}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{2}X_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{2}X_{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{2}X_{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>6</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{2}X_{6}</annotation></semantics></math>, all satisfying strong heredity. The original study used a 12-run Plackett-Burman design. Even at <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=16</annotation></semantics></math>, the interaction-recovery problem is under-identified: a Resolution V fractional factorial requires <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{8-2}=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{8-2}=64</annotation></semantics></math> runs to estimate the <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p+\binom{p}{2}=36" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>36</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p+\binom{p}{2}=36</annotation></semantics></math> terms without aliasing and a modern D-optimal design requires <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="37" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>37</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">37</annotation></semantics></math> runs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goos and Jones, 2011</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We simulate data from the spike-and-slab model of Section 3 with <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\text{active}}=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>active</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\text{active}}=1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\text{inactive}}=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mtext>inactive</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\text{inactive}}=0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.25</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(5,5)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>Beta</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(5,5)</annotation></semantics></math> (prior mean 0.5). Strong heredity is enforced on the interaction indicators. We sweep the budget <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> at three problem sizes: <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\in\{3,4,5,6,8,10,12,16,18,20\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\in\{3,4,5,6,8,10,12,16,18,20\}</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=4</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\in\{6,8,10,12,14,16,18,20,24\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\in\{6,8,10,12,14,16,18,20,24\}</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in\{6,8\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\in\{6,8\}</annotation></semantics></math>. The largest budgets remain well below the Resolution-V threshold noted above. Each policy is evaluated over 100 rollouts on main-effect F1 and interaction F1. TPR and FDR curves for both main effects and interactions are reported in Appendix <a href="#A8.SS3" title="H.3 Case Study 3: metallurgical benchmark (main effects + interactions, 𝑇 sweep at 𝑝∈{4,6,8}) ‣ Appendix H Extended case study results ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The four baselines are as defined in Section 5.1. Two are omitted from this case study. Plackett-Burman is a main-effects-only design whose interaction columns are fully aliased and cannot resolve two-factor interactions. The multi-stage adaptive baseline is likewise main-effects-only. This case study therefore compares DABS against the two baselines whose designs can resolve two-factor interactions: the static sPCE-optimised design and the myopic baseline.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.16927v1/fig_5_3_baselines_F1_main.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:648/186;" width="648" height="186" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Main-effect F1 versus budget <math id="S5.F5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> across problem sizes <math id="S5.F5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in\{4,6,8\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\in\{4,6,8\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Bands are 95% CIs over 5 seeds.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.4 Two-factor interaction screening (metallurgical benchmark) ‣ 5 Results ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows main-effect F1 across the budget sweep. At every problem size <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in\{4,6,8\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\in\{4,6,8\}</annotation></semantics></math>, DABS and the static design track each other closely, with differences of at most 2 to 3 percentage points across most of the range. Both climb monotonically with <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> and approach a common ceiling (F1 <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 0.83" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.83</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 0.83</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=4</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.90" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.90</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.90</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=6</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.93" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.93</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.93</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=8</annotation></semantics></math>). At the smallest budgets, where the design is briefly under-identified for main effects, DABS opens a small edge over the static design (for example at <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=4</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=3</annotation></semantics></math>: DABS <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.59" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.59</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.59</annotation></semantics></math> against static <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.55" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.55</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.55</annotation></semantics></math>), consistent with the wedge prediction from the previous case studies. The myopic baseline lags behind both amortised policies across the sweep, by 10 to 20 percentage points at small budgets and by 5 to 10 percentage points at high budgets.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.16927v1/fig_5_3_baselines_F1_int.png" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:648/186;" width="648" height="186" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Two-factor interaction F1 versus budget <math id="S5.F6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> across problem sizes <math id="S5.F6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\in\{4,6,8\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\in\{4,6,8\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Bands are 95% CIs over 5 seeds.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Main-effect recovery is largely a ceiling story here. The budgets tested cover the identifiable regime for main effects, so DABS and the static design achieve nearly the same expected information gain on <math id="S5.SS4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> and their F1 curves converge. What separates the two amortised policies from the myopic baseline is that both allocate budget with a global view of the sPCE objective, while myopic selects greedily one step at a time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.4 Two-factor interaction screening (metallurgical benchmark) ‣ 5 Results ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> tells a different story. At every problem size, DABS and the static design climb from near-zero interaction F1 at small budgets toward a shared plateau at high <math id="S5.SS4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>: interaction F1 of approximately <math id="S5.SS4.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.37" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.37</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.37</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.SS4.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=4</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S5.SS4.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=20</annotation></semantics></math>), <math id="S5.SS4.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.57" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.57</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.57</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.SS4.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=6</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S5.SS4.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=24" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=24</annotation></semantics></math>), and <math id="S5.SS4.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.70" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.70</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.70</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S5.SS4.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=8</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S5.SS4.p6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=24" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=24</annotation></semantics></math>). The myopic baseline converges to a substantially lower plateau at each <math id="S5.SS4.p6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S5.SS4.p6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.22" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.22</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.22</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS4.p6.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.36" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.36</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.36</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS4.p6.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.46" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.46</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.46</annotation></semantics></math> respectively). The gap between the amortised policies and myopic is large and persistent across the full sweep.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The three-way ordering DABS <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math> Static <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math> Myopic emerges most clearly at <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=6</annotation></semantics></math> in the mid-budget window. At <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=16</annotation></semantics></math>, DABS reaches interaction F1 <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.53" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.53</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.53</annotation></semantics></math> against <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.49" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.49</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.49</annotation></semantics></math> (static) and <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.28" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.28</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.28</annotation></semantics></math> (myopic), and at <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=18" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=18</annotation></semantics></math> the values are <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.56" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.56</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.56</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.51" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.51</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.51</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.39" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.39</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.39</annotation></semantics></math>. Adaptivity alone (myopic) does not close the gap with the well-balanced static design and the static design does not match the DABS target of <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(z;h_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(z;h_{T})</annotation></semantics></math>. What delivers the interaction-recovery gain is a two-phase strategy: DABS uses early experiments to identify candidate active main effects and later experiments to probe the heredity-consistent <math id="S5.SS4.p7.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{i}\xi_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{i}\xi_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> pairs among them. Under strong heredity, DABS can prune the interaction search space only after the active parents have been identified, so its advantage sits in the narrow budget window where mains have just been resolved but the candidate interaction set is not yet saturated. Neither greedy adaptivity nor a fixed balanced design can implement this within a single budget.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The interaction-recovery results confirm that the wedge prediction extends beyond main-effect screening: under strong heredity, the adaptive gain of DABS opens in the mid-budget window where the main-effect subset has just been resolved and the interaction search space has not yet saturated. Beyond these accuracy patterns, DABS is trained offline once and generates each design at deployment in a single forward pass, at the marginal cost of a precomputed static design. Sequential adaptive baselines like the myopic method or multi-stage adaptive procedures require solving a fresh optimisation at every experimental step, which limits their use in time-sensitive workflows.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Ablations &amp; Robustness</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We assess the main design choices in DABS and its robustness to misspecification. We ablate the logit-<math id="S5.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> penalty that prevents policy collapse, the sufficient-statistics encoder against a permutation-invariant MLP encoder, the policy initialisation, the reward structure, and the training objective <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(z;h_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(z;h_{T})</annotation></semantics></math> against the total-information target <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(\theta;h_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(\theta;h_{T})</annotation></semantics></math> used by DAD-style methods. We further evaluate robustness to the observation noise level, to a misspecified sparsity prior, and to a heredity mismatch in which a policy trained under strong heredity is evaluated under weak heredity. A broader hyperparameter sensitivity analysis completes the study. Results and discussion are provided in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Ablations and robustness ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.6 </span>Limitations</h3>

<div id="S5.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training the DABS policy requires substantial upfront computation, particularly for large <math id="S5.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> where the Student-<math id="S5.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> covariance scales as <math id="S5.SS6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> per contrastive sample. This cost is amortised: once trained, a single policy is reused across new experiment instances under the same prior, and the cost-performance trade-off is controlled through the number of training steps and contrastive samples. A second limitation is that the closed-form Student-<math id="S5.SS6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> marginal relies on conjugacy between the spike-and-slab prior and the Gaussian likelihood. Extending DABS to non-conjugate priors or non-Gaussian responses would require likelihood-free contrastive estimators or auxiliary-variable augmentations. Finally, the method assumes a strong-heredity structure for interactions. Its scaling to large <math id="S5.SS6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> is further limited by both network capacity and the cost of training.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper we introduced DABS, a policy-based adaptive Bayesian experimental design method for discrete factorial screening under spike-and-slab priors. By exploiting conjugacy between the prior and likelihood, DABS trains a single policy via Prior Contrastive Estimation on an analytical Student-<math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> marginal and recovers the active factor set through Gibbs posterior inference at deployment. In our experiments, DABS matches or outperforms the strongest non-adaptive Bayesian baseline on a biotechnological screening benchmark, a scaling study with varying dimensionality, and an interaction-recovery benchmark under strong heredity. The largest gains arise precisely where classical orthogonal designs fall short. DABS thereby bridges the gap between modern amortised BOED methods and classical screening practice, enabling efficient adaptive design that directly targets mutual information through a closed-form marginal over the support variables.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Proof of Proposition 1</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Proposition 1 follows from classical convexity arguments in optimal design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pukelsheim, 1993</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kiefer, 1974</a>)</cite>, but we include a proof for completeness and to explicitly adapt the argument to our setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The design space <math id="A1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}=[-1,1]^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}=[-1,1]^{p}</annotation></semantics></math> is a convex polytope whose extreme points are the vertices <math id="A1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{-1,+1\}^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{-1,+1\}^{p}</annotation></semantics></math>. In the linear–Gaussian setting, the mutual information objective can be written as</p>
<table id="A1.E16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\xi)=\tfrac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{\xi^{\top}\Sigma\xi}{\sigma^{2}}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>ξ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ξ</mi></mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\xi)=\tfrac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{\xi^{\top}\Sigma\xi}{\sigma^{2}}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma\succeq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>⪰</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma\succeq 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Since <math id="A1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\mapsto\tfrac{1}{2}\log(1+t/\sigma^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\mapsto\tfrac{1}{2}\log(1+t/\sigma^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> is strictly increasing, maximising <math id="A1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> over <math id="A1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math> is equivalent to maximising the quadratic form <math id="A1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\xi):=\xi^{\top}\Sigma\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ξ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ξ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\xi):=\xi^{\top}\Sigma\xi</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We now show that <math id="A1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\xi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\xi)</annotation></semantics></math> is maximised over <math id="A1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math> at a vertex. Fix all coordinates of <math id="A1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math> except <math id="A1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. The restriction of <math id="A1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is</p>
<table id="A1.E17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\xi_{i})=a\,\xi_{i}^{2}+b\,\xi_{i}+c," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>ξ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\xi_{i})=a\,\xi_{i}^{2}+b\,\xi_{i}+c,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(17)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a=\Sigma_{ii}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a=\Sigma_{ii}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b=2\sum_{j\neq i}\Sigma_{ij}\,\xi_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b=2\sum_{j\neq i}\Sigma_{ij}\,\xi_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is independent of <math id="A1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. This is a convex quadratic function of <math id="A1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> over the interval <math id="A1.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, so its maximum is attained at the boundary <math id="A1.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{i}\in\{-1,+1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{i}\in\{-1,+1\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Applying this argument sequentially to each coordinate shows that any maximiser of <math id="A1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi^{\top}\Sigma\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ξ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ξ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi^{\top}\Sigma\xi</annotation></semantics></math> over <math id="A1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,1]^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,1]^{p}</annotation></semantics></math> lies in <math id="A1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{-1,+1\}^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{-1,+1\}^{p}</annotation></semantics></math>. Since <math id="A1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\xi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\xi)</annotation></semantics></math> is a monotone increasing function of <math id="A1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi^{\top}\Sigma\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ξ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ξ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi^{\top}\Sigma\xi</annotation></semantics></math>, the same holds for <math id="A1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\xi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\xi)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Ablations and robustness</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All ablations in this appendix are anchored on a shared problem class so that effects are directly comparable. We consider <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=10</annotation></semantics></math> candidate factors, budget <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=8</annotation></semantics></math>, observation noise <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> and sparsity prior <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(2,8)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>Beta</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(2,8)</annotation></semantics></math> (prior mean 0.2). Strong heredity is enforced on the interaction indicators. Each policy uses the sufficient-statistics encoder of Section 3.4 and warm-starts from a static sPCE-optimised checkpoint before adaptive fine-tuning. Training runs for 30,000 steps with the recipe of Section 5.3. Each ablation cell is trained with 5 seeds. At evaluation, each policy is rolled out 50 times, decoded by a Gibbs sampler with 200 draws after 100 burn-in steps, with posterior inclusion threshold 0.5. We report main-effect F1 as the primary metric. Interaction F1 is near zero at this problem class because strong heredity combined with the Beta(2, 8) prior yields very few active interactions per instance. The interaction-recovery story is treated in Section 5.4 at a problem class where interactions are prevalent.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This subsection sweeps every real-valued hyperparameter of the training recipe one at a time around the baseline configuration and reports the resulting main-effect F1. Table <a href="#A2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ B.2 Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Appendix B Ablations and robustness ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> aggregates the 25 off-baseline cells into three blocks. The optimisation block covers the learning rate, total number of training steps, exponential learning-rate decay and Adam weight decay. The capacity block covers the encoder hidden dimension and the encoding output dimension. The regularisation and Gumbel-Softmax block covers the logit-<math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> penalty, the diversity bonus, and the three Gumbel-Softmax annealing parameters <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\mathrm{start}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>start</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\mathrm{start}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{\mathrm{end}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>end</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{\mathrm{end}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the anneal fraction. We report main-effect F1 with the standard error over seeds.</p>
</div>

<td id="A2.T1.2.37.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:0.45pt;padding-bottom:0.45pt;"><math id="A2.T1.m74" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.251\pm 0.026" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">0.251</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">±</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">0.026</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.251\pm 0.026</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Hyperparameter sensitivity at <math id="A2.T1.m79" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=10</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.T1.m80" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=8</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.T1.m81" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.5</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.T1.m82" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(2,8)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>Beta</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\sim\mathrm{Beta}(2,8)</annotation></semantics></math></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Across all 25 off-baseline settings in Table <a href="#A2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ B.2 Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Appendix B Ablations and robustness ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, main-effect F1 varies by at most <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.06" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.06</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.06</annotation></semantics></math> relative to the baseline of F1 <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.303\pm 0.017" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>0.303</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.017</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.303\pm 0.017</annotation></semantics></math>. Only two settings drop F1 by more than 1.96 baseline standard errors: an over-aggressive learning rate at <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\times 10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times 10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math> (F1 <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.246\pm 0.018" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>0.246</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.018</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.246\pm 0.018</annotation></semantics></math>) and a small diversity penalty at <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.01</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01</annotation></semantics></math> (F1 <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.247\pm 0.018" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>0.247</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.018</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.247\pm 0.018</annotation></semantics></math>). The remaining 23 settings sit within the noise band of the baseline. Notably, network capacity is not a bottleneck across the ranges tested (hidden dim from 32 to 128, encoding dim from 16 to 64), and the logit-<math id="A2.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> coefficient can be varied over two orders of magnitude (<math id="A2.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.001</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.001</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1</annotation></semantics></math>) without measurable impact. Doubling the training budget from 30,000 to 60,000 steps yields a <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.013" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.013</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.013</annotation></semantics></math> F1 gain, well within one standard error of the baseline, indicating that 30,000 steps is close to the training-time ceiling for this problem class.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Method Ablations and Prior-Mismatch Robustness</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This subsection reports two families of ablations that keep the training recipe fixed while varying either the method or the deployment prior. The first (Table <a href="#A2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ B.3 Method Ablations and Prior-Mismatch Robustness ‣ Appendix B Ablations and robustness ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) varies eleven categorical design choices covering encoder architecture, initialisation, reward structure, regularisation, mutual-information target, observation noise, and heredity assumption at evaluation, and quantifies each choice’s contribution to the baseline F1 of <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.303\pm 0.017" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.303</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.017</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.303\pm 0.017</annotation></semantics></math>. The second (Table <a href="#A2.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ B.3 Method Ablations and Prior-Mismatch Robustness ‣ Appendix B Ablations and robustness ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) evaluates the trained DABS policy on ground-truth data drawn from a mismatched prior, and compares its degradation to that of the static baseline.</p>
</div>

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Method ablations at <math id="A2.T2.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=10</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.T2.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=8</annotation></semantics></math></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The largest effect in Table <a href="#A2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ B.3 Method Ablations and Prior-Mismatch Robustness ‣ Appendix B Ablations and robustness ‣ Deep Adaptive Bayesian Screening" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> is regularisation. Removing the logit-<math id="A2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> penalty collapses F1 from <math id="A2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.303" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.303</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.303</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.080" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.080</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.080</annotation></semantics></math>, a <math id="A2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="74\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>74</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">74\%</annotation></semantics></math> drop. Without the penalty, the Gumbel-Softmax logits saturate early in training and the policy emits a near-constant design, confirming the collapse failure mode described in Section 3.3. Replacing the logit-<math id="A2.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> penalty with a cosine-similarity penalty on consecutive designs does not prevent collapse (F1 <math id="A2.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.147" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.147</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.147</annotation></semantics></math>), and combining both recovers most but not all of the baseline (F1 <math id="A2.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.247" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.247</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.247</annotation></semantics></math>). The logit-<math id="A2.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> penalty is therefore the load-bearing regularisation choice.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The training-objective ablation confirms the chain-rule prediction of Section 3.6. Targeting the total mutual information <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(\theta;h_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(\theta;h_{T})</annotation></semantics></math> as in DAD-style methods yields F1 <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.243" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.243</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.243</annotation></semantics></math>, a reduction of <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.060" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.060</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.060</annotation></semantics></math> from the screening-specific target <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(z;h_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(z;h_{T})</annotation></semantics></math>. Because <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(\theta;h_{T})=I(z;h_{T})+\mathbb{E}_{z}[I(\beta,\sigma^{2};h_{T}\mid z)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(\theta;h_{T})=I(z;h_{T})+\mathbb{E}_{z}[I(\beta,\sigma^{2};h_{T}\mid z)]</annotation></semantics></math> and the conditional term admits no adaptive gain under the linear-Gaussian likelihood, resources spent estimating <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> during training are wasted from the screening perspective. The sufficient-statistics encoder also matters: replacing it with the permutation-invariant MLP encoder of DAD reduces F1 by <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.050" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.050</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.050</annotation></semantics></math>. Warm-starting the policy from the static sPCE-optimised checkpoint adds a further <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.041" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.041</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.041</annotation></semantics></math> over random initialisation. Reward structure (terminal versus dense sPCE) and noise level (<math id="A2.SS3.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 0.017" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>0.017</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 0.017</annotation></semantics></math> across <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\in\{0.25,1.0,2.0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2.0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\in\{0.25,1.0,2.0\}</annotation></semantics></math>) contribute little, and under a heredity mismatch (training under strong heredity, evaluating under weak heredity) F1 drops by only <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.026" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.026</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.026</annotation></semantics></math>, showing that DABS is not brittle to a moderate violation of the training assumption.</p>
</div>

<th id="A2.T3.2.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-top:0.45pt;padding-bottom:0.45pt;"><math id="A2.T3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">π</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi=0.5</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<td id="A2.T3.2.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:0.45pt;padding-bottom:0.45pt;"><math id="A2.T3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.410\pm 0.014" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">0.410</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">±</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">0.014</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.410\pm 0.014</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="A2.T3.2.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:0.45pt;padding-bottom:0.45pt;"><math id="A2.T3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.343" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn mathsize="0.900em">0.343</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.343</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T3.2.7" class="ltx_tr">

<th id="A2.T3.2.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:0.45pt;padding-bottom:0.45pt;"><math id="A2.T3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Beta}(2,8)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">Beta</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">8</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Beta}(2,8)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A2.T3.2.7.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> (matched)</span></th>

<td id="A2.T3.2.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:0.45pt;padding-bottom:0.45pt;"><math id="A2.T3.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.249" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn mathsize="0.900em">0.249</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.249</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T3.2.8" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A2.T3.2.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-top:0.45pt;padding-bottom:0.45pt;"><math id="A2.T3.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Beta}(4,6)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">Beta</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">4</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">6</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Beta}(4,6)</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<td id="A2.T3.2.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:0.45pt;padding-bottom:0.45pt;"><math id="A2.T3.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.381\pm 0.020" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">0.381</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">±</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">0.020</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.381\pm 0.020</annotation></semantics></math></td>
